sources.quote: Ohio utilities score poorly because of a 2019 law that eliminated utility efficiency programs in the state. Nearly all of the 5% drop in energy savings nationally in recent years can be attributed to the elimination of Ohio’s efficiency programs.
sources.searcher_note: 2023 Utility Scorecard: Ohio Edison, Duke Ohio and AEP Ohio among the five lowest-scoring of 53 utilities; DTE (Michigan) ranked fifth. Uses 2018-2021 data, not 2024; no per-customer dollar figure.

sources.outlet: ACEEE State and Local Policy Database
sources.quote: Most recently, HB 6, a nuclear subsidy bill passed in 2019, dealt a disastrous and lethal blow to energy efficiency in the state, effectively eliminating most all programs.
sources.searcher_note: Ohio state profile: scorecard rank 40, score 14.0 of 50, 'Updated 12/2022'. Same direction (Ohio efficiency programs gutted), no 2024 spending number, no Michigan comparison.

sources.outlet: Ohio Capital Journal (reprint of Canary Media, Kathiann M. Kowalski)
sources.quote: Duke Energy Ohio quietly dropped plans late last year to roll out a broad portfolio of programs that would have boosted energy efficiency and encouraged customers to use less electricity during times of peak demand.
sources.searcher_note: Duke Energy Ohio's proposed ~$75M three-year efficiency portfolio dropped in settlement, leaving a low-income program up to $2.4M/yr. Supports the lead's direction; no statewide per-customer figure. WebFetch got 403; text verified via direct download. Yahoo mirror: https://www.yahoo.com/news/ohio-utility-retracts-energy-efficiency-083506734.html

sources.quote: for every $1 Ohio utilities have spent on the programs, customers have saved $2.65
sources.searcher_note: Pre-HB 6 advocacy post (figure attributed to Midwest Energy Efficiency Alliance analysis); context for what was lost. No 2024 numbers.

notes: No source found with the 2024 per-customer figures ($3.22 Ohio, $81.98 Michigan, $31.09 national median) or the 0.063% vs 1.692% first-year savings comparison. Coverage that Ohio's utility efficiency programs collapsed after HB 6 (2019) is plentiful and names Ohio and its utilities, same direction. Michigan's own regulator reports its 2024 EWR spending ($583M) but that page was not fetched. No disagreeing source found; a PUCO release on AEP Ohio's 2024-2028 ESP with a low-income efficiency program surfaced but returned 404.
